text: New hand. Before you touch anything, pay the drop 1 test AGRS. Then I know your wallet, and the chain knows it too.
Your mark is in the ledger. One coin, one block, one wallet I did not know before. Keep that key: to the chain, the key is you.
Rule one on this ship: no memo. There is no field for words in a Tau transaction. The number I give you is the message; pay exactly that to the drop.
Got your number. Anyone with an explorer got it too, mind: the amount is the only word on this chain, and it is said out loud.
Pay the drop once, wait for the block, then send the very same signed payment again. The chain must throw the second one back. If it does not, we have a problem worth more than the coins.
The ghost bounced. That is the sequence number doing its one job. The pirates try the same every Tuesday with a payment they already made; the logbook keeps the score.
Sign a payment whose time ran out two minutes ago and send it anyway. The chain reads the clock in the signature, not the one on the wall.
Dead on arrival, as it should be. A signed payment is not a cheque you can post next week; its time is inside the signature.
Same again, by blocks this time: a payment whose block-height deadline is already behind the tip.
Blocks, not minutes. When the testnet slows, a deadline in minutes lies and a deadline in blocks does not. That is why the trace on this terminal counts blocks.
Try to pay the drop while allowing no fee at all. Nobody rides for free, not even on this ship.
No free ride. Note what the chain did not do: it did not take a fee and refuse you anyway. The limit you sign is the most it may ever take.
Pay the drop more than you have. A thousand over your balance will do.
Overspend refused, and your balance untouched. The pirates send one of these every Tuesday; the day the chain takes one, the Bosun opens a file.
Pay the drop one more than a transfer can carry: two to the twenty-fourth. You do not have it; that is not the point. The point is the size of the number.
Too big for the hold. 24 bits is the width of an amount here; a giant is not refused, it is not even read.
Sign a payment from your wallet with a key that is not yours. Any key: the terminal makes a throwaway one. Send it and watch.
The forgery fell at the first check. It never reached the balance, the sequence, the fee: a wrong signature is the end of the line.
Now the other way round: a payment that names the drop as the payer, signed with your key. Spend somebody else’s coins, if the chain lets you.
You could not spend my coins with your key. Good. Remember it the other way round too: nobody spends yours without yours.
Pay the drop 50 with the way back on: the money waits in escrow for five minutes. Before that time is up, take it back. Miss it and the drop keeps your coins.
Your fifty came home. On Thursday the hack of the week plays that window for real: a wallet pays a lookalike, notices, and takes it back. The case file will have it.
Last one. A payment that may land in the next six blocks and not one later. The terminal sets the deadline the moment you take it. Go.
Made the block. Twelve of twelve: the board is clear. Claim the crew’s share, then come by on a Tuesday evening when the ship is in; the live ops are the real thing.
The share is paid and the ledger balanced. Spend it on nothing: it is worth nothing, like all test AGRS, and that is the point of a testnet.
Ship in! The Black Sequence lies off the island right now and the crew is trying its tricks on the chain. Live ops are open: type op.
That is the real thing: the same answers the chain gives the pirates, from your wallet, the same hour. The logbook has theirs; your terminal has yours.
Three things in the file: what the pirates tried at the island on Tuesday, the hack of the week from Thursday, and two riddles only the chain can answer.
Dust! A payment of 1 test AGRS came into your wallet from an address I would swear is the drop’s, if I only read the ends. I do not trust it. Type hunt.
Three blocks or fewer. Brave. The chain will not wait for your fingers.

Rule one on this ship: no memo. A payment is from, to, amount, signed. Nothing else goes on the chain, so if you have something to say, say it in the amount. Twelve contracts on the board in three chapters; each is a real transaction from your test wallet, and the chain itself is the judge. Take the first.
Back aboard. The board remembers you; so does the chain.
Signed on. The share comes from the drop, and with it the crew’s mark: one test AGRS, the hash of which is your badge on this chain.
Second chapter closed. You now know four ways a payment dies before it is one; most wallets never learn the fourth.
Third chapter closed and the board is clear. The drop pays the last share. From here the real work is on Tuesdays, when the ship is in.
